question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8 non-top-facing stickers are enough, and in practice that's the set most people actually read.

Once OLL is finished the U face is a solid colour, so the top 9 stickers give no information about the permutation. You have to read the side colours of the U-layer pieces. A PLL is a permutation of the four U corners and the four U edges, and after orientation the only distinguishing information left on each piece is on its side stickers.

The four U edges each contribute one visible side sticker on the top row of a side face, four stickers total. The four U corners each contribute two visible side stickers, one on each of the two adjacent side faces. In recognition you never need both stickers of a single corner at the same time – one side sticker per corner already tells you which corner is sitting there, and the other side sticker of that corner is only needed to disambiguate mirror cases. Counting the distinct side stickers you routinely inspect – the three stickers on the front top row and the three stickers on the right top row, plus the two remaining corner side stickers that become visible when you bring the back of the cube into view – the practical recognition set is eight side stickers: the four corner side colours and the four edge side colours of the U layer. With those eight non-U stickers the corner 4-cycle and the edge 4-cycle are both fixed and the 21 PLL cases are distinguishable.

12.text:
In CFOP the U face is finished when you get to the PLL. Up to a whole
cube rotation the U face is therefore monochromatic and it carries no
information at all.  The whole of the PLL information is carried by the
side stickers which belong to the four U–edges and the four U–corners.

The U–layer has

* 4 U–edges, one side sticker per edge,
* 4 U–corners, two side stickers per corner,

i.e. 4+2×4=12 distinct non–U stickers belonging to the last layer.
In principle that is the information you have to be able to read.  In
particular the four edge stickers

E$_{F}$,E$_{R}$,E$_{B}$,E$_{L}$

and one representative side sticker of each of the four U–corners is
enough to tell you which edge is in which U–position and which corner
is in which U–position.  That is the eight distinct side stickers that
are normally quoted, four edges and a representative sticker of each
corner, which is 12 stickers if you count both side stickers of every
corner.

Because a permutation of four objects is fixed by the positions of
three of them, and because the corner parity is the same as the edge
parity in a legal PLL, the fourth edge/corner is in fact forced by the
other seven.  Modulo a whole–cube rotation the 21 PLL classes can be
distinguished by any seven independent non–U stickers of the U–layer,
the usual practical statement being the eight sticker set 4 edges +4
corners, i.e. the 12 side stickers of the U–layer, seven of which are
independent.  This is the information that is normally read off the
three faces F,R,B, i.e. the 3+3=6 U-row stickers you can see at once
and the remaining one after a U-turn. ∎

10.text:
In CFOP the U face is already solved by the time you get to PLL so the
U face itself carries no distinguishing information at all.  What is left
to be distinguished is the permutation of the eight pieces that are now
in the U-slice,

* U4 edge : 1 side sticker per edge,
* U4 corner : 2 side stickers per corner,

i.e. the whole U-slice carries

* 4·1 = 4 edge side stickers and
* 4·2 = 8 corner side stickers

of the top layer, 12 stickers in all, which are the twelve non-U
stickers of the U slice.  In the usual piece–based language this is the
four U edges and the four U corners, i.e. eight distinguishable
U–slice pieces, one side sticker per piece.  Seven of them already
determine the eighth so that in practice a cuber can disambiguate the
21 PLL permutations from the side colours of the eight U–slice pieces,
the familiar six/eight sticker recognition of the top–layer side
colours.  If the two side stickers of a corner are counted separately
that is the 12 non-U stickers of the U slice, 4 + 8, that have to be
read in principle.  This is the eight-piece, twelve-sticker reading
which is normally quoted as “the side colours of the U slice’’ and
it is the whole of the information that is left after OLL.

6.text:
In CFOP the U-face is already colour uniform after OLL.  The only thing
that is still unknown about the last layer is which physical piece is
sitting in which U position.  For a U position the U-colour is known and
the face of the cube is known.  Hence a piece is completely fixed by a
single side sticker

* UF, UR, UB, UL : the piece is U + the colour you see on the front/
  right/ back/ left sticker;
* the four U edges are fixed by the single side sticker that belongs
  to the edge, U + that colour.

So one non-U sticker per U-layer piece is in principle enough to say
which piece is where.  There are eight U-layer pieces, four edges and
four corners, so the information content of the last layer is the
eight side stickers

* 4 × 1 = 4 edge side stickers,
* 4 × 2 = 8 corner side stickers,

12 non-U stickers in all which belong to the U layer.  In particular
one side sticker for each of the eight pieces, i.e. eight non-U
stickers, is information theoretically sufficient to fix the corner
permutation and the edge permutation and hence the 21 PLL classes.
The parity of the U permutation couples corners and edges so that in
practice the four corner-identifying side stickers, the usual
“headlights’’ etc., already determine the case, and in a normal
F/R-hold you are actually looking at the six U-layer side stickers
that lie on the top rows of the front and the right faces, 3+3, from
which the whole PLL class can be read.  This is what is normally quoted
as the 12 stickers of the U layer, 8 of which, and in a standard hold
the six you can see at once, are enough to recognise the PLL. ∎

4.text:
In CFOP the last layer is oriented by the OLL. After the OLL the whole
U face is monochrome. The nine U stickers therefore carry no
information about the permutation. What is left to read is the
permutation of the eight pieces in the U–ring.

The U–ring is

* 4 U edges, each of which contributes one side sticker to the front,
  right, back or left face,  4 stickers;
* 4 U corners, each of which contributes two side stickers, one on each
  of the two side faces that meet the corner,  4×2 = 8 stickers.

Hence the whole information content of a PLL is contained in the
12 side stickers of the U–slice, 8 corner side stickers +4 edge side
stickers.  In a normal single viewpoint you see the 6 side stickers of
the U–ring on the two visible side faces and you rotate the cube to
get the other six; in a single view the eight distinct pieces are
usually quoted as “the four U edges and the four U corners”.

Information-theoretically log2 21 ≃ 4.4 b so more than four stickers
are necessary and seven stickers are enough to separate the 21
essentially different PLLs.  In practice the whole U–ring, i.e. the 12
non-up stickers of the U slice, is what is read, the nine up stickers
being completely uninformative after an OLL.  The 8 piece-wise view is
the one that is usually quoted, 4 edge side stickers + 4 corners, i.e.
12 side stickers in total.

8.text:
In CFOP the OLL step is finished with the U face completely oriented, i.e.
U = * * * * * * * * * .  Apart from the fact that the nine U stickers are
all the same colour there is no information on the U face at all.

Hence the only information that is left in the last layer is the
permutation of the 8 U cubies.  An U edge is completely identified by
the one side sticker that it carries, the U top sticker being known
to be the U colour.  An U corner is completely identified by the two
side stickers that it carries, the U top sticker being known to be the
U colour.  The U ring therefore contains

* 4 U edges × 1 side sticker = 4 side stickers
* 4 U corners × 2 side stickers = 8 side stickers

12 physical non-U stickers in all, i.e. eight distinct U cubies, four
edges and four corners.  In particular the four edge side stickers
U-F, U-R, U-B, U-L and one distinguishing side sticker from each of
the four U corners are enough to name the 8 cubies and hence the
permutation.  The 12-th sticker is then a parity check, so that in
information theoretic terms seven distinct non-U stickers already
determine the PLL class; it is this eight-cubie, twelve-sticker U-ring
that is normally quoted as “the information that has to be read in
PLL’’.  This is usually spoken of as the eight distinctive side
stickers, four edges and four corners, i.e. the twelve physical
stickers of the U ring.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is solved in orientation so the only thing left to distinguish a PLL is which U-layer edge goes where and which U-layer corner goes where. Each of the four U-layer edges is uniquely identified by its single side sticker that sits in the top row of F/R/B/L, and each of the four U-layer corners is uniquely identified by at least one of its two side stickers that sits in the top row of F/R/B/L.

You therefore need one identifying non-U sticker per piece for a complete permutation read. That is four edge stickers plus four corner stickers, 4+4=8 non-top-facing stickers in total. With fewer than that you lose at least one piece identity and mirror/swap ambiguities remain between cases such as U-perms, Z-perm and the H/J perm family, so a full PLL determination is not possible.

17.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochromatic so the top stickers carry no information about which piece is where. A PLL case is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces, four edges and four corners.

Each of the four U edges has exactly one sticker that is not on the top, and that side sticker is visible on the front/back/left/right of the cube. That gives four distinguishing stickers for edges.

Each of the four U corners has two side stickers visible around the U layer, but one side sticker per corner is enough in practice to tell which corner piece is occupying that U position, because the U sticker is already known to be the U colour after OLL. Seeing one distinct side colour per corner is enough to resolve the corner permutation, and in a normal inspection you can see one side sticker for each of the four corners.

So in practice you are reading one non-top sticker for each of the eight U-layer pieces, i.e. four edge side stickers plus four corner side stickers = 8 non-top-facing stickers, which is what is needed to unambiguously name the 21 PLL cases.

21.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8 non-top-facing stickers are enough and in practice are what you end up using. After OLL the U face is monochromatic so all the information for PLL is in the side colours of the U-layer pieces. There are four U-layer edges, each contributes one side sticker, and four U-layer corners, each contributes a distinguishable side sticker to the pattern you recognise – the two visible side colours of a corner are essentially one identifying colour for the piece in the usual headlights/block/antipodal notation. That is 4 + 4 = 8 side stickers in total on the U layer that carry the permutation information. In a fixed view you see a subset of them at once, e.g. the three stickers on the front U-row and the three on the right U-row, but to be able to unambiguously name any of the 21 PLL classes, including the mirror A-perm, E-perm, etc., you have to be able to resolve all four edge positions and all four corner positions, i.e. eight distinct non-U stickers.

15.text:
In CFOP the U face is already solved, so the 9 U stickers are all the same
colour and carry no information about the permutation. The permutation is
what is left on the U layer in the four side faces.

On the U layer you have

* 4 U edges : each edge contributes its one side sticker to the permutation,
  4 stickers;
* 4 U corners : each corner contributes its two side stickers to the
  permutation, 4×2 = 8 stickers;

i.e. the 12 side stickers which belong to the U–layer

         U L R F B
    3·4 =12 side U–layer stickers

The 4 U edges are White–X and the 4 U corners are White–X–Y and after
OLL their orientation is already fixed.  Hence an edge is identified by
the one side colour which is visible on the F B L R top row and a corner
is identified by the ordered pair of its two side colours which is
visible on the F B L R top row.  Up to the trivial redundancy that the
8th cubie is forced by the other seven, those are the 12 non-U stickers
of the last layer which carry the whole PLL information, 8 corner side
stickers and 4 edge side stickers.  In practice one cubie is redundant
so the information theoretic minimum is the 7 independent cubies, 11
independent side stickers, and essentially the eight distinct cubies of
the last layer that you normally read as “the four edge colours and the
four corner colours”.  This is what is normally quoted as the 12-
sticker/8-cubie last-layer read.

19.text:
In CFOP the OLL is finished before the PLL is attacked so that the U face is
monochrome.  The 9 stickers of the U face therefore carry no permutation
information at all.  The whole of the permutation information of the last
layer lives on the side stickers of the eight pieces which are on the U
layer.

On the U layer

* a U edge has one sticker that is not on U;
* a U corner has two stickers that are not on U.

Hence the U layer carries

* 4 edge side stickers
* 4 × 2 = 8 corner side stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers.  Those 12 stickers are the only carriers of the
permutation of the last layer.  In particular the identity of the four
U-edges is the information carried by the four edge side stickers and the
identity of the four U-corners is the information carried by the eight
corner side stickers.  In ordinary recognition one talks about the eight
distinct U pieces, four edges and four corners, i.e. eight distinct non-U
stickers, the twelve side stickers of the U layer being the full
information set.  It is that side information which lets you tell the 21
PLL permutations apart, the nine U stickers being completely uninformative
after OLL.  This is usually quoted as the four edge side stickers plus the
four corner side stickers, i.e. the twelve side stickers of the U layer,
eight distinct pieces, which in practice is recognised from a much smaller
distinguishing set – e.g. four well chosen side stickers are enough to
pin down the edge permutation and with it the corner permutation by parity.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8 non-top-facing stickers are needed for an unambiguous PLL identification in CFOP.

After OLL the U face is uniform so the U stickers themselves give no information about permutation. The only distinguishing information is on the side faces of the U-layer pieces.

For the edges you need the side colour of each of the four U edges. The front, right, back and left side stickers of the four U edges tell you the order of the four edge pieces around the top. That's 4 non-U stickers.

For the corners you also need the side colour of each of the four U corners. One visible side sticker per corner is enough to tell which corner piece sits in which U position, and with AUF accounted for you need the four corners distinguished from each other. That's another 4 non-U stickers.

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top-facing stickers. With those eight you can read the full 4-cycle/swap pattern of corners and edges and pick the correct PLL case, and in practice speedcubers do exactly that by scanning the side colours around the U layer.

1.text:
In CFOP the U face is finished after the OLL step so the nine U stickers are
all the same colour and carry no permutation information.  The only thing
that is left to read is the permutation of the 4 U-edges and the 4 U-corners
in the U-layer.

An U-edge is identified in the U-layer by the one side sticker that it
shows on the four vertical faces, and a U-corner is identified in the
U-layer by the two side stickers that it shows on the two vertical faces
that meet at the corner.  In particular a single side sticker of a U-edge
and a single side sticker of a U-corner is enough to tell which piece is
sitting in a given U-layer position, because the U sticker is already
known to be the solved colour. 

Hence up to a rotation of the cube you have to read

* 4 edge side stickers, one for each of the four U-edges, and
* 4 corner side stickers, one representative side sticker for each of the
  four U-corners,

i.e. eight distinct non-U positions, the information which is in practice
normally seen as the 12 physical side stickers of the U-layer,

4 U-edge side stickers + 4 ×2 U-corner side stickers = 12
non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer,
the four edge stickers and the four front-facing corner stickers being
the eight information-carrying stickers that are normally quoted.  In
particular the four U-edge side stickers alone are enough to fix the
EPLL part of the case and the four U-corner side stickers are enough to
fix the corner permutation, so that with a single view, e.g. the front
U-row 1 edge + 2 corners and the left U-row 1 edge + 2 corners, etc., the
21 PLL classes are distinguished.  It is the conventionally quoted
“8-sticker’’ – 12 physical sticker – read of the U-layer.  If the two
side stickers of each U-corner are counted separately the U-layer has
12 non-U stickers to be inspected.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is uniform so the permutation information is carried entirely by the side colours of the U layer. The U layer contains 8 distinguishable pieces, 4 U corners and 4 U edges. A U edge is identifiable by its single non-U side sticker, and a U corner is identifiable by at least one of its two non-U side stickers; in practice one side sticker per corner is enough to tell which physical corner is in which U position once the top is oriented.

Hence the minimal guaranteed distinguishing set is one side sticker for each of the 8 U pieces, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 non-top-facing stickers. That is the information you actually have to read in the worst case to know which of the 21 PLL permutations you are looking at.

11.text:
In CFOP the F2L is finished and OLL is finished so the U face is
monochrome and the whole of the rest of the cube is already solved.
Up to a rotation of the whole cube the only thing that is still
undetermined is the permutation of the eight pieces of the U–slice.
Four U–edges and four U–corners.

* a U–edge is identified after OLL by its single side colour, the U
colour being common to the four edges.  There are four edge side
stickers in the top row of the four side faces.
* a U–corner is identified after OLL by the unordered pair of its two
side colours.  The two side stickers of a corner lie on the two
adjacent side faces.  There are 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 8
corner side stickers in the top rows of the four side faces.

Hence the information that can change between one PLL and another is
contained in the 4+8 = 12 side stickers which belong to the U–slice,
i.e. in the eight U–layer pieces themselves.  In piece terms this is
the four U–edge side stickers and the four U–corners, eight pieces of
information.  Counting physical stickers the U–slice contributes the
12 non–U stickers

  $4\;{\rm edges}\times1+4\;{\rm corners}\times2=12$

of the top rows of R, F, L, B.  The 9 U stickers are all the same
after OLL and carry no information for the permutation.  In practice
a cuber recognises the case from the four edge side colours together
with one side colour from each of the four corners, i.e. from eight
piece–identifying stickers, twelve physical non–U stickers in all,
and the fourth corner / the fourth edge is then forced by parity.
This is often quoted as the familiar “four edges + four corners = eight
pieces’’ PLL recognition. ∎

3.text:
In CFOP the OLL step has already made the U face monochromatic.  All of
the information which is left to be read in the last layer is therefore
contained in the facelets which belong to the U layer but which lie on the
four side faces of the cube.

On the U layer there are

* 4 U edges.  One facelet of each edge is on U, the other one is on a side
face.  4 side facelets;
* 4 U corners.  One facelet of each corner is on U, the other two are on
side faces.  4×2 = 8 side facelets.

So there are 4+8 = 12 side facelets which belong to the U layer.  Modulo
the 9 monochromatic U facelets those 12 facelets are the whole of the
last layer.  In piece language that is the 4 U edges and the 4 U corners,
8 distinct U layer pieces, whose side colours are the 12 non-U facelets.
In a fixed static view you can only see a fraction of them at once – the
usual two face view U-F-R shows the 3+3=6 distinct non-U U-layer facelets
on the front and right top rows, and by a small U rotation you can see any
of the 12 facelets you want.  That is the 8 piece / 12 facelet information
that is normally quoted as the “8-sticker’’ PLL read, i.e. four edge side
stickers and one distinguishing side sticker per corner, 6 of which are
visible in one static two-face view. ∎

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the top face gives no colour information at all. PLL identification is then a matter of telling the eight U-layer pieces apart by their side colours.

There are four U-layer edges and four U-layer corners. An edge is uniquely identified by its single side sticker and a corner is uniquely identified by at least one of its two side stickers. In the worst case you therefore need one distinguishing side sticker for each of the eight pieces, i.e. four edge side stickers plus four corner side stickers.

In practice you can rotate the cube so the stickers you need come into view, but for a guaranteed identification you have to be able to see one non-U sticker for every U-layer piece, 8 stickers in total. Once those eight side colours are known the top permutation is fixed and the PLL case is determined.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 4

In CFOP the U layer is already orientation solved after OLL, so PLL is pure permutation. The permutation can be read off the U face, and the only information that is not already contained in the U stickers themselves is which edge piece is sitting in each U edge slot. That is given by the single side sticker that belongs to each of the four U edges. Once you know the four edge side colours you know the edge cycle, and the corner cycle is forced by parity on the U layer, so the 21 PLL cases are uniquely determined. In practice most people just glance at those four side stickers together with the U face and that is enough to tell an Aa from an Ab, a U from a Z, etc. The corner side stickers are redundant for case identification once the edges are known.

16.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 4

In CFOP the top is OLL-solved so orientation is already fixed. The permutation of the last layer is then entirely encoded in which piece sits on each U-layer slot. The U stickers alone give you the cycle structure of the four U corners and the four U edges, and the only remaining ambiguity is the absolute identity of the edge pieces between the two mirror versions of a given cycle. 

Once you have fixed the cube rotation, the four U-layer edges are all distinguishable from their single side stickers on the front, right, back and left faces. With those four side colors you can confirm which edge is which and therefore which edge permutation you have, and the corner permutation follows from the U face. In practice you only ever need to glance at the front four stickers of the U layer – two U corners and two U edges on the front – i.e. four non-U stickers to break the mirror ambiguity and lock the exact PLL case.

20.text:
In CFOP after OLL the $U$ face is monochrome.  The only information that
is left in the last layer is the $U$–slice permutation.  The $U$ slice
contains

* 4 $U$ edges  $E_{U}$ : one sticker of each edge is visible on the
four side faces,
* 4 $U$ corners $C_{U}$ : two side stickers of each corner are visible
on the four side faces.

Hence on the four side faces the top row is made up of

$$4\;{\rm edge\;side\;stickers}+4\times 2\;{\rm corner\;side\;stickers}=12$$

non-$U$ stickers, viz. the 12 stickers of the $U$–slice that are not on
the $U$ face.  It is the colour pattern carried by those 12 stickers
that distinguishes the 21 $U$–slice permutations, up to the $C_{4}$
rotation of the cube about the $U$ axis.  In particular the edge
permutation is carried by the four edge side stickers and the corner
permutation is carried by the eight corner side stickers.  Up to the
$C_{4}$ rotational equivalence and the edge–corner parity the
permutation is already fixed by the four edge side colours and one side
colour per corner, i.e. in practice by $4+4=8$ distinct side stickers,
$7$ independent stickers being enough in the worst case.  The twelve
stickers above are the twelve physically distinct non-$U$ stickers of
the $U$ slice that contain the whole PLL information.  This is the
$8$ piece, $12$ sticker set that is normally quoted as the $U$–slice
side information for PLL recognition.

18.text:
In CFOP the U-face is already oriented by the OLL step so that the whole
U face is of one colour. All of the information that distinguishes one
PLL from another is therefore carried by the side stickers of the eight
pieces that are in the U-layer.

On the U layer there are

* 4 U-edges : 1 non-U sticker per edge
* 4 U-corners : 2 non-U stickers per corner

i.e. 4+8 = 12 stickers which belong to the U layer but do not lie on the
U face.  It is those 12 side stickers which carry the permutation
information.  In information terms a single identifying side sticker is
enough to name an U-edge and one identifying side sticker is enough to
name an U-corner up to the relative position of the two side colours, so
that in practice the 21 PLLs can be distinguished by the 8 distinct
U-layer pieces

4 U-edges ×1 + 4 U-corners ×1 = 8

distinct non-U stickers, the 12 stickers being the 4×1+4×2 side stickers
of the whole U layer.  This is normally quoted as the 12 side stickers
of the top layer, 8 of which are the conventional `one per piece'
recognising set.

U–slice pieces, one side sticker per piece.  Seven of them already
determine the eighth so that in practice a cuber can disambiguate the
21 PLL permutations from the side colours of the eight U–slice pieces,
the familiar six/eight sticker recognition of the top–layer side
colours.  If the two side stickers of a corner are counted separately
that is the 12 non-U stickers of the U slice, 4 + 8, that have to be
read in principle.  This is the eight-piece, twelve-sticker reading
which is normally quoted as “the side colours of the U slice’’ and
it is the whole of the information that is left after OLL.
public_text.6:
In CFOP the U-face is already colour uniform after OLL.  The only thing
that is still unknown about the last layer is which physical piece is
sitting in which U position.  For a U position the U-colour is known and
the face of the cube is known.  Hence a piece is completely fixed by a
single side sticker

* UF, UR, UB, UL : the piece is U + the colour you see on the front/
  right/ back/ left sticker;
* the four U edges are fixed by the single side sticker that belongs
  to the edge, U + that colour.

So one non-U sticker per U-layer piece is in principle enough to say
which piece is where.  There are eight U-layer pieces, four edges and
four corners, so the information content of the last layer is the
eight side stickers

* 4 × 1 = 4 edge side stickers,
* 4 × 2 = 8 corner side stickers,

12 non-U stickers in all which belong to the U layer.  In particular
one side sticker for each of the eight pieces, i.e. eight non-U
stickers, is information theoretically sufficient to fix the corner
permutation and the edge permutation and hence the 21 PLL classes.
The parity of the U permutation couples corners and edges so that in
practice the four corner-identifying side stickers, the usual
“headlights’’ etc., already determine the case, and in a normal
F/R-hold you are actually looking at the six U-layer side stickers
that lie on the top rows of the front and the right faces, 3+3, from
which the whole PLL class can be read.  This is what is normally quoted
as the 12 stickers of the U layer, 8 of which, and in a standard hold
the six you can see at once, are enough to recognise the PLL. ∎
public_text.4:
In CFOP the last layer is oriented by the OLL. After the OLL the whole
U face is monochrome. The nine U stickers therefore carry no
information about the permutation. What is left to read is the
permutation of the eight pieces in the U–ring.

The U–ring is

* 4 U edges, each of which contributes one side sticker to the front,
  right, back or left face,  4 stickers;
* 4 U corners, each of which contributes two side stickers, one on each
  of the two side faces that meet the corner,  4×2 = 8 stickers.

Hence the whole information content of a PLL is contained in the
12 side stickers of the U–slice, 8 corner side stickers +4 edge side
stickers.  In a normal single viewpoint you see the 6 side stickers of
the U–ring on the two visible side faces and you rotate the cube to
get the other six; in a single view the eight distinct pieces are
usually quoted as “the four U edges and the four U corners”.

Information-theoretically log2 21 ≃ 4.4 b so more than four stickers
are necessary and seven stickers are enough to separate the 21
essentially different PLLs.  In practice the whole U–ring, i.e. the 12
non-up stickers of the U slice, is what is read, the nine up stickers
being completely uninformative after an OLL.  The 8 piece-wise view is
the one that is usually quoted, 4 edge side stickers + 4 corners, i.e.
12 side stickers in total.
public_text.8:
In CFOP the OLL step is finished with the U face completely oriented, i.e.
U = * * * * * * * * * .  Apart from the fact that the nine U stickers are
all the same colour there is no information on the U face at all.

Hence the only information that is left in the last layer is the
permutation of the 8 U cubies.  An U edge is completely identified by
the one side sticker that it carries, the U top sticker being known
to be the U colour.  An U corner is completely identified by the two
side stickers that it carries, the U top sticker being known to be the
U colour.  The U ring therefore contains

* 4 U edges × 1 side sticker = 4 side stickers
* 4 U corners × 2 side stickers = 8 side stickers

12 physical non-U stickers in all, i.e. eight distinct U cubies, four
edges and four corners.  In particular the four edge side stickers
U-F, U-R, U-B, U-L and one distinguishing side sticker from each of
the four U corners are enough to name the 8 cubies and hence the
permutation.  The 12-th sticker is then a parity check, so that in
information theoretic terms seven distinct non-U stickers already
determine the PLL class; it is this eight-cubie, twelve-sticker U-ring
that is normally quoted as “the information that has to be read in
PLL’’.  This is usually spoken of as the eight distinctive side
stickers, four edges and four corners, i.e. the twelve physical
stickers of the U ring.
public_text.13:
8

After OLL the U face is solved in orientation so the only thing left to distinguish a PLL is which U-layer edge goes where and which U-layer corner goes where. Each of the four U-layer edges is uniquely identified by its single side sticker that sits in the top row of F/R/B/L, and each of the four U-layer corners is uniquely identified by at least one of its two side stickers that sits in the top row of F/R/B/L.

You therefore need one identifying non-U sticker per piece for a complete permutation read. That is four edge stickers plus four corner stickers, 4+4=8 non-top-facing stickers in total. With fewer than that you lose at least one piece identity and mirror/swap ambiguities remain between cases such as U-perms, Z-perm and the H/J perm family, so a full PLL determination is not possible.
public_text.17:
8

After OLL the U face is monochromatic so the top stickers carry no information about which piece is where. A PLL case is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces, four edges and four corners.

Each of the four U edges has exactly one sticker that is not on the top, and that side sticker is visible on the front/back/left/right of the cube. That gives four distinguishing stickers for edges.

Each of the four U corners has two side stickers visible around the U layer, but one side sticker per corner is enough in practice to tell which corner piece is occupying that U position, because the U sticker is already known to be the U colour after OLL. Seeing one distinct side colour per corner is enough to resolve the corner permutation, and in a normal inspection you can see one side sticker for each of the four corners.

So in practice you are reading one non-top sticker for each of the eight U-layer pieces, i.e. four edge side stickers plus four corner side stickers = 8 non-top-facing stickers, which is what is needed to unambiguously name the 21 PLL cases.
public_text.21: 8 non-top-facing stickers are enough and in practice are what you end up using. After OLL the U face is monochromatic so all the information for PLL is in the side colours of the U-layer pieces. There are four U-layer edges, each contributes one side sticker, and four U-layer corners, each contributes a distinguishable side sticker to the pattern you recognise – the two visible side colours of a corner are essentially one identifying colour for the piece in the usual headlights/block/antipodal notation. That is 4 + 4 = 8 side stickers in total on the U layer that carry the permutation information. In a fixed view you see a subset of them at once, e.g. the three stickers on the front U-row and the three on the right U-row, but to be able to unambiguously name any of the 21 PLL classes, including the mirror A-perm, E-perm, etc., you have to be able to resolve all four edge positions and all four corner positions, i.e. eight distinct non-U stickers.
public_text.15:
In CFOP the U face is already solved, so the 9 U stickers are all the same
colour and carry no information about the permutation. The permutation is
what is left on the U layer in the four side faces.

On the U layer you have

* 4 U edges : each edge contributes its one side sticker to the permutation,
  4 stickers;
* 4 U corners : each corner contributes its two side stickers to the
  permutation, 4×2 = 8 stickers;

i.e. the 12 side stickers which belong to the U–layer

         U L R F B
    3·4 =12 side U–layer stickers

The 4 U edges are White–X and the 4 U corners are White–X–Y and after
OLL their orientation is already fixed.  Hence an edge is identified by
the one side colour which is visible on the F B L R top row and a corner
is identified by the ordered pair of its two side colours which is
visible on the F B L R top row.  Up to the trivial redundancy that the
8th cubie is forced by the other seven, those are the 12 non-U stickers
of the last layer which carry the whole PLL information, 8 corner side
stickers and 4 edge side stickers.  In practice one cubie is redundant
so the information theoretic minimum is the 7 independent cubies, 11
independent side stickers, and essentially the eight distinct cubies of
the last layer that you normally read as “the four edge colours and the
four corner colours”.  This is what is normally quoted as the 12-
sticker/8-cubie last-layer read.
public_text.19:
In CFOP the OLL is finished before the PLL is attacked so that the U face is
monochrome.  The 9 stickers of the U face therefore carry no permutation
information at all.  The whole of the permutation information of the last
layer lives on the side stickers of the eight pieces which are on the U
layer.

On the U layer

* a U edge has one sticker that is not on U;
* a U corner has two stickers that are not on U.

Hence the U layer carries

* 4 edge side stickers
* 4 × 2 = 8 corner side stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers.  Those 12 stickers are the only carriers of the
permutation of the last layer.  In particular the identity of the four
U-edges is the information carried by the four edge side stickers and the
identity of the four U-corners is the information carried by the eight
corner side stickers.  In ordinary recognition one talks about the eight
distinct U pieces, four edges and four corners, i.e. eight distinct non-U
stickers, the twelve side stickers of the U layer being the full
information set.  It is that side information which lets you tell the 21
PLL permutations apart, the nine U stickers being completely uninformative
after OLL.  This is usually quoted as the four edge side stickers plus the
four corner side stickers, i.e. the twelve side stickers of the U layer,
eight distinct pieces, which in practice is recognised from a much smaller
distinguishing set – e.g. four well chosen side stickers are enough to
pin down the edge permutation and with it the corner permutation by parity.
public_text.5:
8 non-top-facing stickers are needed for an unambiguous PLL identification in CFOP.

After OLL the U face is uniform so the U stickers themselves give no information about permutation. The only distinguishing information is on the side faces of the U-layer pieces.

For the edges you need the side colour of each of the four U edges. The front, right, back and left side stickers of the four U edges tell you the order of the four edge pieces around the top. That's 4 non-U stickers.

For the corners you also need the side colour of each of the four U corners. One visible side sticker per corner is enough to tell which corner piece sits in which U position, and with AUF accounted for you need the four corners distinguished from each other. That's another 4 non-U stickers.

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top-facing stickers. With those eight you can read the full 4-cycle/swap pattern of corners and edges and pick the correct PLL case, and in practice speedcubers do exactly that by scanning the side colours around the U layer.
public_text.1:
In CFOP the U face is finished after the OLL step so the nine U stickers are
all the same colour and carry no permutation information.  The only thing
that is left to read is the permutation of the 4 U-edges and the 4 U-corners
in the U-layer.

An U-edge is identified in the U-layer by the one side sticker that it
shows on the four vertical faces, and a U-corner is identified in the
U-layer by the two side stickers that it shows on the two vertical faces
that meet at the corner.  In particular a single side sticker of a U-edge
and a single side sticker of a U-corner is enough to tell which piece is
sitting in a given U-layer position, because the U sticker is already
known to be the solved colour. 

Hence up to a rotation of the cube you have to read

* 4 edge side stickers, one for each of the four U-edges, and
* 4 corner side stickers, one representative side sticker for each of the
  four U-corners,

i.e. eight distinct non-U positions, the information which is in practice
normally seen as the 12 physical side stickers of the U-layer,

4 U-edge side stickers + 4 ×2 U-corner side stickers = 12
non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer,
the four edge stickers and the four front-facing corner stickers being
the eight information-carrying stickers that are normally quoted.  In
particular the four U-edge side stickers alone are enough to fix the
EPLL part of the case and the four U-corner side stickers are enough to
fix the corner permutation, so that with a single view, e.g. the front
U-row 1 edge + 2 corners and the left U-row 1 edge + 2 corners, etc., the
21 PLL classes are distinguished.  It is the conventionally quoted
“8-sticker’’ – 12 physical sticker – read of the U-layer.  If the two
side stickers of each U-corner are counted separately the U-layer has
12 non-U stickers to be inspected.
public_text.7:
8

After OLL the U face is uniform so the permutation information is carried entirely by the side colours of the U layer. The U layer contains 8 distinguishable pieces, 4 U corners and 4 U edges. A U edge is identifiable by its single non-U side sticker, and a U corner is identifiable by at least one of its two non-U side stickers; in practice one side sticker per corner is enough to tell which physical corner is in which U position once the top is oriented.

Hence the minimal guaranteed distinguishing set is one side sticker for each of the 8 U pieces, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 non-top-facing stickers. That is the information you actually have to read in the worst case to know which of the 21 PLL permutations you are looking at.
public_text.11:
In CFOP the F2L is finished and OLL is finished so the U face is
monochrome and the whole of the rest of the cube is already solved.
Up to a rotation of the whole cube the only thing that is still
undetermined is the permutation of the eight pieces of the U–slice.
Four U–edges and four U–corners.

* a U–edge is identified after OLL by its single side colour, the U
colour being common to the four edges.  There are four edge side
stickers in the top row of the four side faces.
* a U–corner is identified after OLL by the unordered pair of its two
side colours.  The two side stickers of a corner lie on the two
adjacent side faces.  There are 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 8
corner side stickers in the top rows of the four side faces.

Hence the information that can change between one PLL and another is
contained in the 4+8 = 12 side stickers which belong to the U–slice,
i.e. in the eight U–layer pieces themselves.  In piece terms this is
the four U–edge side stickers and the four U–corners, eight pieces of
information.  Counting physical stickers the U–slice contributes the
12 non–U stickers

  $4\;{\rm edges}\times1+4\;{\rm corners}\times2=12$

of the top rows of R, F, L, B.  The 9 U stickers are all the same
after OLL and carry no information for the permutation.  In practice
a cuber recognises the case from the four edge side colours together
with one side colour from each of the four corners, i.e. from eight
piece–identifying stickers, twelve physical non–U stickers in all,
and the fourth corner / the fourth edge is then forced by parity.
This is often quoted as the familiar “four edges + four corners = eight
pieces’’ PLL recognition. ∎
public_text.3:
In CFOP the OLL step has already made the U face monochromatic.  All of
the information which is left to be read in the last layer is therefore
contained in the facelets which belong to the U layer but which lie on the
four side faces of the cube.

On the U layer there are

* 4 U edges.  One facelet of each edge is on U, the other one is on a side
face.  4 side facelets;
* 4 U corners.  One facelet of each corner is on U, the other two are on
side faces.  4×2 = 8 side facelets.

So there are 4+8 = 12 side facelets which belong to the U layer.  Modulo
the 9 monochromatic U facelets those 12 facelets are the whole of the
last layer.  In piece language that is the 4 U edges and the 4 U corners,
8 distinct U layer pieces, whose side colours are the 12 non-U facelets.
In a fixed static view you can only see a fraction of them at once – the
usual two face view U-F-R shows the 3+3=6 distinct non-U U-layer facelets
on the front and right top rows, and by a small U rotation you can see any
of the 12 facelets you want.  That is the 8 piece / 12 facelet information
that is normally quoted as the “8-sticker’’ PLL read, i.e. four edge side
stickers and one distinguishing side sticker per corner, 6 of which are
visible in one static two-face view. ∎
public_text.9:
8

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the top face gives no colour information at all. PLL identification is then a matter of telling the eight U-layer pieces apart by their side colours.

There are four U-layer edges and four U-layer corners. An edge is uniquely identified by its single side sticker and a corner is uniquely identified by at least one of its two side stickers. In the worst case you therefore need one distinguishing side sticker for each of the eight pieces, i.e. four edge side stickers plus four corner side stickers.

In practice you can rotate the cube so the stickers you need come into view, but for a guaranteed identification you have to be able to see one non-U sticker for every U-layer piece, 8 stickers in total. Once those eight side colours are known the top permutation is fixed and the PLL case is determined.
public_text.14:
4

In CFOP the U layer is already orientation solved after OLL, so PLL is pure permutation. The permutation can be read off the U face, and the only information that is not already contained in the U stickers themselves is which edge piece is sitting in each U edge slot. That is given by the single side sticker that belongs to each of the four U edges. Once you know the four edge side colours you know the edge cycle, and the corner cycle is forced by parity on the U layer, so the 21 PLL cases are uniquely determined. In practice most people just glance at those four side stickers together with the U face and that is enough to tell an Aa from an Ab, a U from a Z, etc. The corner side stickers are redundant for case identification once the edges are known.
public_text.16:
4

In CFOP the top is OLL-solved so orientation is already fixed. The permutation of the last layer is then entirely encoded in which piece sits on each U-layer slot. The U stickers alone give you the cycle structure of the four U corners and the four U edges, and the only remaining ambiguity is the absolute identity of the edge pieces between the two mirror versions of a given cycle. 

Once you have fixed the cube rotation, the four U-layer edges are all distinguishable from their single side stickers on the front, right, back and left faces. With those four side colors you can confirm which edge is which and therefore which edge permutation you have, and the corner permutation follows from the U face. In practice you only ever need to glance at the front four stickers of the U layer – two U corners and two U edges on the front – i.e. four non-U stickers to break the mirror ambiguity and lock the exact PLL case.
public_text.20:
In CFOP after OLL the $U$ face is monochrome.  The only information that
is left in the last layer is the $U$–slice permutation.  The $U$ slice
contains

* 4 $U$ edges  $E_{U}$ : one sticker of each edge is visible on the
four side faces,
* 4 $U$ corners $C_{U}$ : two side stickers of each corner are visible
on the four side faces.

Hence on the four side faces the top row is made up of

$$4\;{\rm edge\;side\;stickers}+4\times 2\;{\rm corner\;side\;stickers}=12$$

non-$U$ stickers, viz. the 12 stickers of the $U$–slice that are not on
the $U$ face.  It is the colour pattern carried by those 12 stickers
that distinguishes the 21 $U$–slice permutations, up to the $C_{4}$
rotation of the cube about the $U$ axis.  In particular the edge
permutation is carried by the four edge side stickers and the corner
permutation is carried by the eight corner side stickers.  Up to the
$C_{4}$ rotational equivalence and the edge–corner parity the
permutation is already fixed by the four edge side colours and one side
colour per corner, i.e. in practice by $4+4=8$ distinct side stickers,
$7$ independent stickers being enough in the worst case.  The twelve
stickers above are the twelve physically distinct non-$U$ stickers of
the $U$ slice that contain the whole PLL information.  This is the
$8$ piece, $12$ sticker set that is normally quoted as the $U$–slice
side information for PLL recognition.
public_text.18:
In CFOP the U-face is already oriented by the OLL step so that the whole
U face is of one colour. All of the information that distinguishes one
PLL from another is therefore carried by the side stickers of the eight
pieces that are in the U-layer.

On the U layer there are

* 4 U-edges : 1 non-U sticker per edge
* 4 U-corners : 2 non-U stickers per corner

i.e. 4+8 = 12 stickers which belong to the U layer but do not lie on the
U face.  It is those 12 side stickers which carry the permutation
information.  In information terms a single identifying side sticker is
enough to name an U-edge and one identifying side sticker is enough to
name an U-corner up to the relative position of the two side colours, so
that in practice the 21 PLLs can be distinguished by the 8 distinct
U-layer pieces

4 U-edges ×1 + 4 U-corners ×1 = 8

distinct non-U stickers, the 12 stickers being the 4×1+4×2 side stickers
of the whole U layer.  This is normally quoted as the 12 side stickers
of the top layer, 8 of which are the conventional `one per piece'
recognising set.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is about PLL recognition after OLL in CFOP. U face is monochrome after OLL so the 9 U stickers carry no permutation information. All PLL information lives in the U-slice side stickers.

Consensus points:
* U-slice has 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.
* A U-edge contributes 1 non-U side sticker, a U-corner contributes 2 non-U side stickers.
* Physical non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer = 4×1 + 4×2 = 12 stickers, the top rows of R,F,L,B.
* The nine U stickers are uninformative.

Disagreement on counting:
* Piece-based view: one identifying side sticker per U piece is enough to name the piece because the U colour is known. That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top-facing stickers, the usual “8-sticker” / “8-piece” quote.
* Full physical view: counting both side stickers of each corner gives 12 non-U stickers of the U-layer. This is the whole information content.
* Information-theoretic minimality: parity couples corners and edges, so the 8th piece is forced by the other seven; log2 21 ≈4.4 bits, so in principle 7 independent non-U stickers suffice to separate the 21 classes, with a C4 rotation equivalence.
* Edge-only claim: Colleagues 14,16 argue 4 edge side stickers are enough because corner permutation follows from edge parity. This is contested by the majority who say mirror/swap ambiguities remain without corner side information, e.g. U-perm vs Z-perm, A-perm vs Ab etc.

Current understanding: In practice cubers read the side colours of the eight U-layer pieces, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 representative corner side stickers = 8 non-top-facing stickers, which corresponds physically to the 12 side stickers of the U-layer. The minimal guaranteed distinguishing set is commonly quoted as 8, with 12 being the physical count and 7 being the information-theoretic lower bound. The 4-sticker claim is an outlier and appears to rely on parity forcing but is disputed.

Unresolved: whether the question wants the physical 12-sticker count, the practical 8-sticker piece-identifying count, or the information-theoretic minimum 7. The phrasing “must be seen” suggests minimal sufficient set, i.e. 8 distinct stickers, 12 physical stickers total.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is PLL recognition after OLL in CFOP. After OLL the U face is monochromatic so the 9 U stickers carry no permutation information. All PLL information lives on the side stickers of the U-slice.

Commonly agreed facts from round 0:
* U-slice = 4 U-edges + 4 U-corners = 8 pieces.
* A U-edge contributes 1 non-U sticker, visible on the top row of F/R/B/L.
* A U-corner contributes 2 non-U stickers, visible on the top rows of its two adjacent side faces.
* Hence the U-slice physically contains 4×1 + 4×2 = 12 non-U stickers. Those 12 are the 12 side facelets of the U-row.

Agreement on the conventional reading:
* Edge permutation is read from the 4 edge side stickers.
* Corner permutation is read from the 8 corner side stickers, but one representative side sticker per corner is enough in practice to name the piece because the U sticker is known.
* This is normally quoted as the 8-piece / 12-sticker U-ring read: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct piece-identifying stickers, 12 physical stickers counting both corner sides.

Divergences noted:
* 8 vs 12 counting. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,8 quote the 12 physical non-U stickers of the U-layer, with the 8 distinct piece-identifying stickers as the practical set.
* Colleagues 13,17,7,9,5,2,21,6,8 insist the minimal guaranteed distinguishing set is 8 non-top stickers, one per U-layer piece.
* Colleagues 14,16 argue 4 edge side stickers are enough because corner parity follows edge parity in a legal PLL; they claim the corner side stickers are redundant. This is contested by the majority.
* Information-theoretic minimality is mentioned: log2 21 ≈ 4.4 bits, seven independent non-U stickers suffice in principle, the eighth is forced by parity/rotation.

Current understanding: U face gives zero info. Full physical information is the 12 non-U stickers of the U-slice. In piece language the usual practical statement is 8 distinct non-top stickers, 4 edge + 4 corner, with 12 physical stickers counting both sides of each corner. The 4-edge-only claim is a minority view and appears to lose mirror/swap ambiguities such as U vs Z, A vs Ab etc. Unresolved is whether the question asks for physical sticker count 12 or distinct piece-identifying count 8.

15.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP state at PLL entry is OLL-solved, so the nine U stickers are monochromatic and carry no permutation information. All distinguishing information is in the U-slice side stickers.

The U-slice contains 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.
* Each U-edge contributes 1 non-U sticker visible on the top row of F/R/B/L.
* Each U-corner contributes 2 non-U stickers visible on the two adjacent side faces.

Hence physically the U layer has 4·1 + 4·2 = 12 non-U stickers, the 12 side stickers of the top row of the four side faces. That is the full information set normally quoted as the U-ring.

In piece terms the information is 8 U-layer pieces. After OLL the U colour is known, so an edge is identified by its single side colour and a corner is identified by at least one of its two side colours. In practice recognition is described as one identifying non-U sticker per piece: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top stickers. The 12 physical stickers contain redundancy: the second side sticker of each corner and the eighth cubie are forced by parity.

Information-theoretic minimum is lower: a permutation of four objects is fixed by three positions and edge-corner parity couples the two sets, so seven independent non-U stickers are enough to separate the 21 PLL classes. Some colleagues argue for the extreme 4-edge view, claiming corner permutation follows from edge permutation by parity and cube rotation, i.e. 4 edge side stickers suffice in principle. The dominant public view in round 0 is 8 distinct / 12 physical stickers, with the usual practical statement 8 stickers = 4 edges + 4 corners, 12 physical side stickers of the U slice.

Unresolved tension: counting physical stickers vs counting distinct identifying stickers, and whether the minimal guaranteed worst-case number is 8 or 7. No previous private belief to revise; first round establishes the 12-physical / 8-distinct baseline and the minority 4-sticker claim.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: After OLL the U face is monochrome in CFOP, so the 9 U stickers carry no permutation information. The remaining information is the permutation of the 8 U-slice pieces: 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.

* Piece counting: each U-edge contributes 1 non-U side sticker, 4×1=4; each U-corner contributes 2 non-U side stickers, 4×2=8. The U-slice therefore contains 4+8=12 physical non-U stickers, i.e. the top rows of F,R,B,L. This is the full physical set repeatedly quoted by colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20.

* Distinguishing counting: one side sticker per piece is enough to name the piece once the U colour is known. That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner identifying side stickers =8 distinct non-top-facing stickers. 3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is about PLL information after OLL in CFOP. U is monochrome, the 9 U stickers carry no permutation information. The only remaining information is the permutation of the 8 U-layer pieces: 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.

The U-slice physically contains

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U edge stickers
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 non-U corner stickers

i.e. 4+8 = 12 non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer, the 12 stickers of the top rows of R,F,L,B. In piece language that is 8 distinguishable U-layer pieces.

In recognition practice one identifying side colour per piece is normally quoted. An U-edge is identified by its single side colour; a U-corner is identified up to piece identity by at least one of its two side colours because the U sticker is already known after OLL. That gives the conventionally quoted 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U stickers, 12 physical stickers when both sides of each corner are counted. The eighth piece is redundant by parity, so information-theoretically 7 independent non-U stickers suffice to separate the 21 PLL classes, up to a C4 rotation of the whole cube.

The 4-edge-only claim is a minority view. Edge permutation alone is 6 possibilities and corner permutation alone is 6 possibilities; parity couples them but does not make the corner permutation a function of the edge permutation. Cases such as A-perm vs E-perm, or U-perm vs Z-perm, etc., need corner information as well as edge information, so four edge side stickers alone cannot disambiguate the full 21 PLL classes.

Unresolved nuance: counting physical stickers vs piece-identifying stickers. The physically distinct information resides in the 12 non-U U-layer stickers; the practically quoted recognising set is the 8 piece-identifying stickers, 4 edges + 4 corners, with the 12-sticker count being the full physical set. This matches the majority of colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,21,2,3,4,6,8. The 4-sticker claims of colleagues 14,16 are inconsistent with the need to resolve corner permutations.

Each U-edge is fixed by its one side sticker in the top row of F/R/U/B/L and each U-corner is fixed by its two side stickers in the top rows of the two adjacent side faces. In piece terms you need one identifying non-U sticker for each of the eight U-layer pieces:

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4
* 4 U-corners × 1 representative side sticker = 4

4 + 4 = 8 distinct non-top-facing stickers. Counting both side stickers of a corner that is the 4 + 4×2 = 12 physical non-U stickers of the U-slice.

In a normal F/R hold you do see 3+3 = 6 non-U U-layer stickers at once, and a U turn brings the remaining stickers into view. That is why people talk about “six at a glance”. It is not the guaranteed identifying set. For the mirror pairs A-perm / A’ , J-perm / J’ , U-perm / U’ , etc., and for Z-perm vs H-perm discrimination you need a representative side colour from all four corners and all four edges. With fewer than eight distinct pieces you retain mirror / swap ambiguity. identifying non-U stickers,

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry no permutation information. PLL is the permutation of the eight U-slice cubies.

On the U-slice we have

* 4 U-edges : 1 side sticker per edge in the top row of F/R/B/L
* 4 U-corners : 2 side stickers per corner in the top rows of F/R/B/L

i.e. 4·1 + 4·2 = 12 physical non-U facelets belong to the U-ring. In piece language that is the four U-edges and the four U-corners.

The U colour is known after OLL so a U-edge is named by its single side colour and a U-corner is named by one representative side colour, the second side colour of the corner being fixed by the known U colour up to parity. One identifying non-U sticker per U-layer piece is therefore the conventional piece-based read:

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top-facing, piece-identifying stickers.

Those eight stickers are the information carried by the twelve physical U-ring stickers. With those eight you can name all four edge positions and all four corner positions and you break the mirror/swap ambiguities that survive on edge information alone: U-perm mirror, A-perm / A’a, Z-perm vs H/J family, etc.

The 3+3 = 6 stickers you can see at once in a normal F/R hold is a visibility statement, not an identification guarantee. It leaves the back edge and the back corner unseen and it does not resolve the mirror pairs until a U-turn brings the remaining U positions into view. Four edge side stickers alone do not fix the corner permutation.

So the guaranteed, rotation-invariant read of the 21 PLL classes is the eight-piece, twelve-physical-sticker U-ring: eight distinct non-U stickers, four edges + four corners, the twelve side facelets of the top rows of F,R,B,L being the full physical realisation.

A U-corner is named by the two side stickers it shows on its two adjacent side faces; once the U colour is known one representative side sticker per corner is enough to know which physical corner is in that U position, the second side sticker being the parity check.

Hence in piece terms the guaranteed, rotation-invariant read of PLL is one identifying non-U sticker for each of the eight U-layer pieces:

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4
* 4 U-corners × 1 representative side sticker = 4

4 + 4 = 8 distinct non-top-facing, piece-identifying stickers. Physically those eight pieces realise 4×1 + 4×2 = 12 non-U facelets in the top rows of F,R,B,L, the usual 12-sticker U ring.

The 3 + 3 = 6 stickers you can see at once in a normal F/R hold is a visibility limitation, not the information requirement. That six-sticker window covers three front U-row facelets and three right U-row facelets; it does not contain a distinguishing side colour for the back-left U-edge and the back-left U-corner. Mirror/swap ambiguities remain until those pieces are also resolved:

* U-perm vs U-perm mirror, A-perm vs a-perm, E-perm variants,
* Z-perm vs H-perm vs J-perm family,

are not disambiguated by edges alone, nor by the six-sticker F/R window alone. You need a representative side colour from all four corners and all four edges. Four edge stickers alone, and six stickers in a single static view, do not break those mirror cases.
